Over the past month, Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) stock has gained 16%, a run that leaves the rest of enterprise software well behind. Palantir stock is down 4% to $201.31 today, however, and this pullback could clarify the choice between taking profits and adding more. A sector-wide rally would have pulled the whole group closer to the pace of Palantir stock, but the month's figures show a far wider spread, with Salesforce stock, ServiceNow stock and the software fund all lagging and the gap pointing to forces specific to Palantir.

title: Salesforce vs. Palantir Technologies: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
detail:
Salesforce vs. Palantir Technologies: Which Technology Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
Pamela Kock, The Motley Fool

CRM
PLTR
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Choosing between Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) and Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) requires weighing mature, steady cash flow against high-octane growth. Both companies are now central players in the evolving landscape of enterprise software.

Salesforce focuses on managing customer relationships through a massive cloud ecosystem, while Palantir provides the underlying operating systems for data-driven decision-making. Investors often compare them because both are aggressively integrating artificial intelligence into their core offerings to capture a larger share of corporate IT budgets.

The case for Salesforce

Among tech stocks, Salesforce provides a comprehensive suite of cloud-based tools, including its Customer 360 platform and the newly launched Agentforce. The company serves a diverse global audience across sectors like financial services and healthcare, recently expanding its data capabilities through the acquisition of Informatica. No single customer accounts for more than 10% of revenue, providing a stable foundation for its subscription model.

In the fiscal year ended Jan. 31, 2026, revenue reached nearly $41.5 billion, representing a year-over-year increase of roughly 9.6%. This steady growth was accompanied by net income of approximately $7.5 billion, showing a net margin of close to 18%. These results show the company is transitioning from pure revenue expansion toward more robust bottom-line profitability.

As of its January 2026 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 0.3x, showing the company uses a conservative amount of debt relative to its equity. The current ratio, which measures the ability to pay short-term obligations with short-term assets, is roughly 0.8x, and free cash flow reached nearly $14.4 billion in its latest fiscal year. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 23.4% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for Palantir Technologies

Palantir builds specialized platforms like Foundry and Gotham that allow organizations to integrate massive data sets for real-time analysis. Its Artificial Intelligence Platform (AIP) has become a primary growth driver, helping it reach over 1,000 total customers. However, the company faces customer concentration risk, as its top three clients accounted for approximately 16% of total revenue in its most recent annual report.

In the fiscal year ended Dec. 31, 2025, revenue reached nearly $4.5 billion, a significant jump of roughly 56.2% compared with the prior fiscal year. The company reported net income of approximately $1.6 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 36.3%. This surge in profitability highlights the scalability of its software platforms as more commercial enterprises adopt its AI tools.

title: Michael Burry Is Bearish on Palantir, Which Is Up 19% Over the Past Year, but His Oracle Short Just Got a Boost From a 53% Stock Drop. Is His AI Bubble Bet Still Worth Following?
detail:
Michael Burry Is Bearish on Palantir, Which Is Up 19% Over the Past Year, but His Oracle Short Just Got a Boost From a 53% Stock Drop. Is His AI Bubble Bet Still Worth Following?
Jennifer Saibil, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 6:15 AM CDT 4 min read
PLTR
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Michael Burry has become one of the most-followed investors in the market. Although he disbanded his hedge fund, Scion Capital, late last year, he still invests. He also frequently shares his thoughts on the market and various stocks on his Substack, Cassandra Unchained, and on social media.

He's made no secret of his views on overinvestment in artificial intelligence (AI) and overpriced AI stocks. In one of his most recent posts on X, he warned that, "By early 2000, 70-80% of stocks were in bear markets, and the indexes continued to move higher. I have a word for that. Denial."

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Michael Burry. Image source: Getty Images.

To that end, he's made several short bets against some of the biggest and most important AI stocks. Given that Burry made his original fortune by betting against the U.S. real estate market ahead of the 2008 mortgage crisis -- a prescient gamble that was later chronicled in Michael Lewis's book The Big Short and the film of the same name -- this is his game.

However, so far, some of his recent bearish bets have not paid off. He has puts on Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ: PLTR), and Oracle (NYSE: ORCL), among others, but those stocks have not all sunk in the way that he hoped they would. Does that mean it's time for his followers to move on?

Is the market in denial?

Burry says the market is in denial, and asserts that borrowed money is propping it up. He also says that ahead of other recent crashes, the "denial stage" lasted six to nine months.

He's buying solid retail stocks like MercadoLibre and Deckers Outdoor, but he's still short on several major AI stocks, including Nvidia, Palantir, and Oracle. He's been publicly negative about Nvidia, casting doubt on the math it's using to describe the depreciation rate of its chips, and what those used chips will be worth over time. He rolled his original Nvidia puts over into new ones with September 2027 expiration dates, and his Palantir and Oracle options expire in September 2027 and December 2027, respectively.

His first public disclosure of his Nvidia and Palantir positions was made while he was still running Scion Asset Management last year. The Nvidia puts were revealed in the first quarter, while the Palantir puts were revealed in the third quarter. The Oracle position is more recent, and was disclosed in January of this year.

Palantir Technologies has ridden a powerful AI and defense story into fresh all time highs, which raises a straightforward question for you as an investor. Is the current share price still grounded in the cash flows the business can realistically produce, or has sentiment pulled ahead of the underlying economics?

Over the past 3 years the stock has returned very roughly 11x, which puts a large premium on the idea that future cash flows will justify the move.

New projects in sovereign AI, including the Regna AI venture and expanding defense and commercial partnerships, can reshape expectations for how quickly Palantir converts revenue opportunities into durable cash generation.

The issue now is whether Palantir's current market value is supported by the cash flows implied by a Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) view of the business.

If you are weighing Palantir Technologies after this AI fueled run, it can help to cross check the story against other 92 AI infrastructure stocks.

Does Palantir Technologies Look Pricey on Cash Flow?

The Discounted Cash Flow (DCF) approach here takes Palantir Technologies' latest twelve month free cash flow of about $3.36b and projects it forward based on rising cash generation. Those projections assume that free cash flow keeps growing through the next decade, then settles into a slower second stage as the business matures.

On those inputs, the DCF output suggests Palantir's estimated intrinsic value sits modestly below the current share price of $208.67, which implies the market is already paying up for that long runway of projected cash flows. The launch of Regna AI as a dedicated sovereign AI venture helps explain why investors are comfortable assigning a premium, since it ties Palantir more tightly to defense and national security budgets.
